narrative:
The model predicted a 62% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. Being in the third decile means you placed in the bottom 30% of your class that year, noticeably lower than the average rank of accepted students. Your first-year class rank was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; you again ranked in the third decile, compared with an average of sixth decile among those who were admitted.

Your family income bracket was the second most influential piece of information. Coming from an upper-middle income family slightly increased the model’s estimate of bar exam failure risk, even though this is the most common income group among accepted students.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed your solid LSAT score of 34, your 3.10 undergraduate GPA, and your plan to attend full-time.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or enroll in a post-baccalaureate program, and consider reapplying once you can demonstrate higher class rankings. You may also want to explore schools with different admissions thresholds or seek advising on bar exam preparation resources that target students with similar profiles.
